Introduction to Rise Up

For Section B of your OCR Drama exam, you must write about a live theatre performance you have seen. You need to analyse and evaluate the acting, design elements, and how meaning was communicated to the audience.

The performance you watched was ‘Rise Up’ by Lisa Evans for the Theatre Centre, performed at Unity College’s Auditorium. Section B is an essay question worth 30 marks — 20 marks for answering the question and 10 marks for using drama terminology. You have 30 minutes to write your response.

Key Fact — Section B Requirements

Every Section B answer must state the name of the play, where you watched it, and when. You will be asked to either analyse or evaluate an aspect of the performance. Always include: a clear example of what you observed, why it was effective, its impact on you and the audience, and how it could be developed.

Key Fact — Paragraph Structure for Section B

Every paragraph in your Section B answer must follow this structure:

  • Thumbs up (Positive): Give an example of something that was successful and justify why it was effective.
  • Thumb towards yourself (Impact): Explain the impact on you or the audience — what did it make you think, feel, or understand?
  • Thumbs down (Development): Suggest a development and justify why that change would be even more effective.

Remember: every paragraph needs all three — positive, impact, and development.

Synopsis: The Freedom Riders

‘Rise Up’ is a play within a play. A group of four British actors meet to discuss and educate the audience about the Freedom Riders of 1960s America. The play explores how a group of Black and White protesters set off on an epic journey from Washington to the Southern States of America to expose racism.

Despite laws making segregation illegal, Black people were still not welcome in White establishments and were not allowed to sit where they wished on buses and coaches. The Freedom Riders wanted to show that this discrimination was still happening. They encountered violent racist protests in which some lost their lives and were often arrested or dumped in Ku Klux Klan territories by the police — despite having the backing of the American government.

The play explores several important themes:

  • Equality and Racism — the central focus, demonstrated by the Freedom Riders’ journey and the violent opposition they faced
  • Relationships — shown through the bonds between the Freedom Riders, and between the Little White Girl and her racist family
  • Violence — demonstrated by the attack on the Freedom Riders’ bus in Birmingham, Alabama
  • Ambitions — shown through Diane Nash’s determination to achieve equality through non-violent protest

Style: Abstract with Naturalism

The playwright states at the start: “Form: Fluid storytelling in which actors can move from character to character with precise and efficient movement. The piece should be played with truth but not naturalistically.”

The style of the play was abstract, with moments of naturalism. This allowed the audience to see how the characters felt and interacted with each other. The abstract style meant performers faced out towards the audience and used symbolic staging rather than realistic settings.

Key Fact — Genre

Rise Up is documentary drama. All the information is based on documented evidence and facts about the real Freedom Riders, though some names were changed to protect characters. It is also educational and informative, designed to teach the audience about what actually happened in 1960s America. The meaning of the play is to encourage audiences to solve problems without violence and to question their own opinions and beliefs.

The Cast

Rise Up was performed by just four actors who used multi-rolling to portray many different characters throughout the performance:

  • Em (Emma Dennis-Edwards) — a Black female performer who played multiple roles including a Freedom Rider in the bus explosion and an old Black lady offering refuge
  • CJ (Sam Kacher) — the only White performer, who played Governor Patterson, Bobby Kennedy, and the Little White Girl
  • Dayz (Kimisha Lewis) — a Black female performer who played Diane Nash and a Freedom Rider on the bus
  • Ty (Edward Nkom) — a Black male performer who played Uncle George, Jim, and a young Freedom Rider

The performance used several drama conventions that you should reference in your exam:

  • Narration — actors stepped out of character to narrate events directly to the audience, helping them understand the context
  • Flashback — used to show historical events such as Diane Nash addressing students at Fisk University
  • Sound collage — multiple voices speaking simultaneously to build tension and create a climax
  • Ensemble movement — actors moving in synchronisation to show unity or to mark key moments
  • Choral work — actors speaking in unison to show shared opinions (e.g. the White shoppers)
  • Facing out — all performers face the audience, reinforcing the abstract style
  • Marking the moment — slow motion used during the bus explosion to emphasise its significance

Writing Your Opening Paragraph

Every Section B response must begin with a summarising paragraph. This helps the examiner put the play into context and shows your understanding. Here is an example:

“I watched the play ‘Rise Up’ by Lisa Evans for the Theatre Centre, at Unity College’s Auditorium. The play explores the fight against racism in America in the 1960s. A group of Blacks and Whites, the Freedom Riders, set off on an epic journey from Washington to the Southern States of America to expose racism. They wanted to show, despite laws making segregation illegal, that Blacks were still not welcome in White establishments and were not allowed to sit where they wished on buses and coaches.”

The SEAS Paragraph Structure

Every paragraph in your Section B essay should follow the SEAS structure:

  • S — State what you observed (a clear example from the performance)
  • E — Explain why it was effective, using drama terminology
  • A — Audience — discuss the impact on you and the audience
  • S — Suggest a development — how could it have been improved and why?
Key Fact — Useful Evaluation Phrases

Build these phrases into your writing: “This was effective because…”, “In my opinion I thought…”, “However, in reflection…”, “I particularly enjoyed…”, and “I feel that this could have been developed because…”

before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Voice skills (Clarity, Tone, Pace, Pitch, Accent, Pause, Volume, Emphasis) and physicality skills (eye contact, facial expression, posture, muscle tension, gesture, body language, gait, levels, proximity) must be named using correct terminology in the exam.
  • Semiotics is the study of signs and symbols on stage — everything from costume colour to proxemics creates meaning for the audience.
  • Use the COSTUMES framework (Context, Opinion, Style, Time Period, Uber/location, Materials, Examples, Semiotics) to structure design answers and ensure you cover all the elements the examiner is looking for.
